prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A Load of brushes and baskets and cradles and chairs Labours along the street in the rain: With it a man, a woman, a pony with whiteybrown hairs. — The man foots in front of the horse with a shambling sway At a slower tread than a funeral train, While to a dirge-like tune he chants his wares, Swinging a Turk's-head brush (in a drum-major's way When the bandsmen march and play). A yard from the back of the man is the whiteybrown pony's nose: He mirrors his master in every item of pace and pose: He stops when the man stops, without being told, And seems to be eased by a pause; too plainly he's old, Indeed, not strength enough shows To steer the disjointed waggon straight, Which wriggles left and right in a rambling line, Deflected thus by its own warp and weight, And pushing the pony with it in each incline. The woman walks on the pavement verge, Parallel to the man: She wears an apron white and wide in span, And carries a like Turk's-head, but more in nursing-wise: Now and then she joins in his dirge, But as if her thoughts were on distant things, The rain clams her apron till it clings. — So, step by step, they move with their merchandize, And nobody buys.

outputs.L1:
A load of brushes, baskets, cradles, and chairs labours along the rain-wet street. With it go a man, a woman, and a pony with whitey-brown hair.

The man walks before the horse with a shambling sway, moving at a pace slower than a funeral train. To a dirge-like tune, he chants his wares, swinging a Turk’s-head brush like a drum-major when the bandsmen march and play.

A yard behind him is the whitey-brown pony’s nose. The animal mirrors his master in every detail of pace and posture: he stops when the man stops, without being told, and seems relieved by each pause. He is plainly old, with scarcely enough strength to steer the disjointed wagon straight. The wagon wriggles left and right in a rambling line, deflected by its own warp and weight, pushing the pony with it at every incline.

The woman walks along the edge of the pavement, parallel to the man. She wears a wide white apron and carries a similar Turk’s-head brush, though more as one might cradle something in a nursing way. Now and then she joins in his dirge, but as though her thoughts are fixed on distant things. The rain clams her apron until it clings.

So, step by step, they move on with their merchandise—and nobody buys.
outputs.L2:
A cart piled high with brushes, baskets, cradles, and chairs  
makes its heavy way down the rainy street.  
Beside it are a man, a woman, and a white-brown pony.  

The man trudges ahead of the animal with an uneven, lurching motion,  
moving more slowly than a funeral procession.  
As he goes, he calls out his goods in a mournful, dirge-like voice,  
waving a Turk’s-head brush as though he were a drum-major  
leading musicians on parade.  

Just behind him, about a yard away, comes the pony’s white-brown muzzle.  
The animal copies its owner exactly in speed and posture:  
when the man halts, the pony halts too, needing no command,  
and the rest seems welcome to him. He is clearly very old.  
He has too little strength left to keep the loose-jointed wagon running straight.  
The cart twists and veers from side to side in a wandering course,  
pulled off by its own crookedness and weight,  
and at every slant it shoves the pony along with it.  

The woman keeps to the edge of the pavement,  
walking level with the man.  
She wears a broad white apron,  
and she carries another Turk’s-head brush, holding it almost as if nursing it.  
From time to time she adds her voice to his mournful cry,  
though she seems to be thinking of faraway matters.  
The rain soaks her apron, making it stick to her.  

And so, little by little, they continue onward with their goods,  
but no one purchases anything.
outputs.L3:
A man, a woman, and an old white-brown pony moved slowly along the rainy street, making their way through the wet and dreary afternoon. Behind the pony rattled a warped little wagon, piled high with brushes, baskets, cradles, and chairs. The load looked awkward and heavy, and every movement seemed to demand effort from both the animal and the people walking beside it.

The man went in front of the pony, leading the way at a steady, weary pace. As he walked, he called out his wares in a long, mournful chant. His voice rose and fell like a dirge, carrying through the rain with a sad, repetitive rhythm. It was less like a sales cry than a lament, as though he had sung the same words too many times to hope they would bring him any fortune.

The old pony followed close behind him, matching not only the man’s pace but even the small changes in his movement. When the man slowed, the pony slowed; when he shifted, the pony seemed to shift with him. Its white-brown coat was dulled by age and rain, and it looked exhausted, barely strong enough to pull the crooked wagon along the street. Each step suggested patience rather than strength.

Beside them walked the woman, carrying a brush in her hand. From time to time she joined the man’s chant, adding her voice to his, but she seemed only half-present. Her attention appeared to drift away from the street and the goods they were trying to sell. She walked with them, yet there was a distant, distracted quality about her, as if her thoughts were somewhere far beyond the rain and the slow turning wheels.

Together, the three of them continued their difficult progress through the wet street: the man chanting, the pony straining forward, and the woman walking beside them with her brush. But despite their effort, their load of useful things, and their repeated calls, no one came out to buy. The rain kept falling, the street remained indifferent, and they moved on without selling a single item.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a bleak, rain-soaked street scene in which poverty and endurance are placed on display. A poor man, a woman, and an old pony move slowly through the wet streets, hauling a cart loaded with household wares. As they pass, they call out their goods in a repeated, chant-like cry, trying to attract buyers. The sound of their voices, the steady movement of the pony, and the miserable weather create the feeling of a mournful procession rather than ordinary street trade.

The man, woman, and pony seem exhausted, worn down by labor and age, yet they continue their difficult routine because they have no other choice. Their goods may be useful and their need is obvious, but the people around them remain unmoved. The repeated idea that “nobody buys” becomes the emotional center of the poem. It shows not only that their work is unsuccessful, but also that their suffering is ignored.

Through this scene, the poem emphasizes poverty, futility, and social indifference. The rain makes the street feel cold and hopeless, while the slow movement of the cart suggests a life trapped in repetition. The people continue to work, advertise, and endure, but nothing changes. Their effort does not lead to relief, and their appeals do not bring help. In the end, the poem’s power comes from this harsh realization: despite their persistence and need, the world passes them by.

**Sharing the Load With Labours**

Every project becomes easier when people work together. A heavy load can be difficult for one person to carry alone, but with labours working as a team, the task becomes faster and safer. Whether it is construction, farming, transportation, or factory work, labourers play an important role in completing daily tasks.

Labours help move materials, carry tools, prepare work areas, and support skilled workers. Their effort reduces the load on others and keeps the work moving smoothly. With proper planning, fair wages, safety equipment, and respect, labourers can perform their duties more effectively.

In any workplace, success depends not only on machines or money, but also on the hard work of people. When we share the load with labours and value their contribution, we create a stronger, more productive, and more respectful working environment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholy narrative poem in the style of Thomas Hardy about street hawkers selling household wares in the rain, with a man, woman, old pony, and overloaded wagon.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Hawkers in the Rain**

Along the street, where lamp-flames swam  
Like ghosts in yellow blurs,  
There went a wagon, bowed and crammed  
With basins, pans, and furs;  
Tin kettles clashed at every jolt,  
And pails gave out a cry,  
As though the load had grief in it  
And could not travel by.

An old grey pony, ribbed and wet,  
With forelock to his eyes,  
Pulled on as one who had forgot  
The worth of greener skies;  
His hoofs made dull replies against  
The stones’ unsheltered stain,  
And from his flanks the water ran  
Like memories of rain.

Beside him walked a weary man,  
His coat at shoulder torn,  
Who cried, “Fine wares for hearth and home!”  
But not as in the morn;  
His voice fell flat against the doors  
Where curtains kept the light,  
And every window seemed to say,  
“We buy no dreams to-night.”

A woman, shawled about the chin,  
Went calling through the weather,  
With wooden spoons and plates of tin  
Bound clattering together;  
Her face was not yet old, but bore  
That look the poor folk take—  
As if they hear, before it comes,  
The sound their hearts will make.

“Good pans! New brooms! A warming pot!  
A jug without a flaw!”  
The man cried on, though all he got  
Was rain for thanks, and raw;  
And sometimes, where a doorway gaped,  
A child would pause to see  
The shining wares, the patient beast,  
The strange sad pageantry.

Then on they moved, past chapel wall,  
Past shop and shuttered inn,  
The wagon heaped with household hopes  
No house would gather in;  
And still the rain wrote slanting lines  
On crate and wheel and mane,  
As if the heavens kept account  
Of all that asked in vain.

I watched them till the mist and dark  
Made one of load and limb—  
The woman’s shawl, the pony’s back,  
The man’s hat, soaked and dim;  
And thought how lives may creak along,  
Overburdened, poor, and slow,  
Selling small comforts in the rain  
They never come to know.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Victorian-style poem describing a brush-and-basket seller slowly moving through a rainy street, using archaic diction, close visual detail, and a bleak ending.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Brush-and-Basket Man**

Adown the lane, where leaden gutters wept,  
And lamps, like dying tapers, blurred the mire,  
A grey old man his mournful errand kept,  
Bent ’neath his load as under God’s own ire.  

Upon his back the osier baskets hung,  
Their pallid ribs with rain all darkly glossed;  
And from his arm the brooms and brushes swung,  
Like woodland trophies from some battle lost.  

His hat, wide-brimmed and bruised by many a year,  
Drooped o’er a brow the weather had made wan;  
The rain ran silver at his cheek and ear,  
And in his beard the sooty droplets shone.  

“Fine brushes—baskets—who will buy?” he cried,  
Yet not a casement stirred its curtained gloom;  
The shuttered houses kept their warmth inside,  
And left him with the drizzle and the doom.  

The kennel gurgled by his broken shoe;  
His coat clung close, a rag of sable skin;  
The wheels went past and splashed him through and through,  
But none looked forth to bid the pedlar in.  

Slow, slow he moved, as though each stone did hold  
Some memory of a hunger long endured;  
His trembling fingers, livid with the cold,  
Still touched his wares, as if their sale were assured.  

A child’s face peeped, then vanished from the pane;  
A dog howled once beneath a dripping stair;  
The church-clock smote its iron through the rain,  
And left the hour to perish in the air.  

At last he reached the bridge, where vapours creep  
From out the river’s black and breathless flow;  
He set his baskets down as one for sleep,  
And watched the yellow lamps shake far below.  

No buyer came. The rain, with patient thread,  
Stitched roof to road and river unto sky.  
At morn they found his brushes by him spread—  
Unsold, unwarmed; and no man wondered why.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that imitates Thomas Hardy’s “A Load of Brushes” tone and meter, focusing on poverty, age, rain, and people passing without buying anything.
counterfactuals.output:
**No Sale**

The rain came slant on market-day,  
And blurred the inn-sign’s red;  
Old Jabez stood with brooms to sell,  
A sacking on his head.  

Beside him, tied with tarry cord,  
The heather-brushes lay,  
As brown and lean as winter birds  
Upon a hedge of grey.  

“Good besoms here!” he called at first,  
With what old strength he had;  
But wheels went by, and boots went by,  
And faces, dry and glad.  

The women drew their shawls more close,  
The farmers eyed the sky;  
A lad laughed out, “No sweeping now—  
The rain will wash us by.”  

So hour by hour the water ran  
From brim to beard and chin;  
His coat grew dark, his fingers blue,  
His hollow cheeks fell in.  

He thought of bread upon a shelf,  
Of embers failing red,  
Of one who coughed beside the wall  
And asked if he had sped.  

But none would buy a broom that day,  
Though all had mire at door;  
They passed with pennies warm in hand  
And left him three times poor.  

At dusk he shouldered up the load,  
More heavy than at morn:  
The sticks were light, the weight was years,  
And hope, too long outworn.  

The rain went with him down the lane,  
Past thorn and dripping stone;  
And all the town, swept clean with rain,  
Let the old man go alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed, somber poem about an old pony pulling a crooked wagon full of baskets, cradles, chairs, and brushes while its owners chant their wares.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Pony of the Crooked Wagon**

Down the road where the rain had hardened  
into ruts like old scars in the clay,  
an aged pony drew a crooked wagon  
at the gray, thin end of day.

His mane hung low in muddied strings,  
his coat was dull with dust and burrs,  
and every bone beneath his hide  
seemed older than the road was.

The harness creaked across his shoulders,  
patched with twine and blackened leather;  
the iron bit was cold with spit,  
the reins were stiff with weather.

Behind him lurched the listing cart,  
one wheel higher, one wheel lame,  
its boards bent out like weary ribs,  
its axle groaning out his name.

There were baskets stacked like empty nests,  
willow-woven, pale and fraying;  
cradles fit for dreamless infants,  
rocking softly, though none were swaying.

Chairs with rush seats, cracked and faded,  
leaned together, back to back,  
like townsfolk waiting out a funeral  
dressed in varnish, dust, and lack.

Brushes bristled in their bundles—  
scrub and hearth and horsehair brooms—  
made to sweep the world to order,  
made to clear the corners’ gloom.

And on the wagon’s sagging tailboard,  
beneath a tarpaulin stained with rain,  
a dozen little household hopes  
knocked softly, knocking, once again.

“Baskets! Cradles! Chairs and brushes!”  
the owners cried along the lane,  
their voices flat as market bells  
that ring and ring and bring no change.

“Fine strong baskets! Rocking cradles!  
Chairs for hearth and brushes new!”  
They chanted as if hunger taught them  
every word they ever knew.

A man walked beside the pony,  
boots sunk deep in roadside mire;  
his beard was silvered, eyes were hollow,  
his breath went smoking like a fire.

A woman perched among the wares,  
wrapped in shawls of brown and black,  
her hands red-knuckled, clasped around  
a ledger folded in a sack.

She sang the prices to the houses,  
to shuttered glass and bolted doors;  
her voice went up to empty windows,  
then fell unanswered to the floors.

For no one came with coins or welcome,  
no child ran out, no housewife called;  
only the crows in the wet elm branches  
shifted, muttered, watched them all.

Still the pony dragged the wagon  
past the mill and chapel stone,  
past the field where nothing ripened,  
past the well left dry and lone.

His hooves came down with careful sorrow,  
one by one, a patient sound,  
as though he feared to wake the dead  
that slept beneath the frozen ground.

Once, perhaps, he had been nimble,  
had cantered bright through summer grass,  
with sunlight warm upon his withers  
and flies like sparks around him pass.

Once, perhaps, a child had fed him  
apple peels with open palms,  
and braided flowers through his forelock  
on mornings clear and blue with psalms.

But now the road was long and narrowing,  
the fields were brown, the ditches filled,  
and every hill became a judgment  
passed on lungs and legs and will.

The wagon swayed and clattered after,  
full of things for human need:  
beds for babies, seats for suppers,  
tools to scour and tubs to clean.

All the tender, common comforts—  
woven, carved, and bound with straw—  
rode behind that trembling creature  
like the weight of human law.

“Baskets! Cradles! Chairs and brushes!”  
cried the woman, cried the man,  
not with hope, but habit only,  
as the daylight thinned and ran.

Their chant went wandering through the village,  
worn as threadbare cloth is worn;  
it had the sadness of a cradle  
waiting for a child unborn.

It had the ache of empty chairs  
set round a table stripped of bread,  
the whisper of a brush at morning  
sweeping ashes from the dead.

And the pony heard, or seemed to hear it,  
that brittle litany of trade,  
while the crooked wagon leaned behind him  
like a debt that must be paid.

At the bridge he stopped a moment;  
water black beneath him shone.  
The man said nothing, only rested  
one cracked hand upon his bone.

No kindness large enough to save him,  
no pasture waiting past the bend,  
only dusk and road and burden,  
only labor without end.

Then onward, with the harness tightening,  
onward through the smoky air,  
past the last lamp in the window,  
past the last unanswered prayer.

The baskets knocked like hollow questions.  
The cradles rocked with no reply.  
The chairs looked out with splintered patience.  
The brushes bristled toward the sky.

And still the owners called their wares  
to houses sunk in evening’s breath:  
“Baskets! Cradles! Chairs and brushes!”—  
a song half commerce and half death.

Long after they had passed from seeing,  
when fog had taken cart and man,  
the pony’s hoofbeats seemed to linger  
where the darkened road began.

Slow, uneven, faint, retreating,  
bearing what the poor must bear:  
the crooked wagon, the unsold comforts,  
and the cold weight of despair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Hardy-esque street scene in verse: a man and woman hawk brushes in the rain, an exhausted pony follows, the wagon sways, and the poem ends with “And nobody buys.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the grey, griping rain of a market-day street,  
Where the gutters ran yellow and wide,  
A man and a woman with sorrow-soaked feet  
Cried brushes from side unto side.  

“Fine brooms for the hearth, and soft brushes for clothes!”  
They called through the clatter and hiss;  
But the shutters were drawn, and the lamps in wet rows  
Blurred each face that had nothing to miss.  

Behind them a pony, rib-shadowed and worn,  
Went nodding as though in a dream;  
Its mane clung in cords, and its head hung forlorn  
By the shafts’ slow shudder and creak.  

The wagon lurched after, rain-blackened and bare,  
With handles and bristles a-sway,  
While the woman’s thin bonnet sagged down on her hair,  
And the man’s voice grew hoarser than day.  

So they passed by the windows where warm people sat,  
Past the inn with its ember-red eyes;  
And the rain wrote their fortune on coat, wheel, and hat—  
And nobody buys.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
